{{Short description|Marketing measurement metric}}
In [[advertising]], a '''gross rating point''' ('''GRP''') measures the size of an audience that an advertisement impacts.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2018-05-24 |title=Gross Rating Point (GRP) {{!}} Universal Marketing Dictionary |url=https://marketing-dictionary.org/g/gross-rating-point/ |access-date=2024-01-27 |language=en-US}}</ref> GRPs help answer ''how often'' "must someone see it before they can readily recall it" and "how many times" does it take before the desired outcome occurs.<ref name=GRP.NYT76>{{cite news
|newspaper=[[The New York Times]]
|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1976/06/22/archives/advertising-on-frequency-and-effectiveness.html
|title=Advertising  |author=Philip H. Dougherty |date=June 22, 1976}}</ref>

==Overview==
Gross rating points are a measure of the impact by a campaign using a specific [[Media (communication)|medium]] or schedule.  It quantifies [[Cost per impression|impressions]] as a percentage of the target population, multiplied by [[Frequency (marketing)|frequency]]. This percentage may be greater, or in fact much greater, than 100.

[[Target rating point]]s express the same concept, but with regard to a more narrowly defined target audience.<ref name=Marketing_Metrics>Farris, Paul W.; Neil T. Bendle; Phillip E. Pfeifer; David J. Reibstein (2010). ''Marketing Metrics: The Definitive Guide to Measuring Marketing Performance.'' Upper Saddle River, New Jersey: Pearson Education, Inc. {{ISBN|0-13-705829-2}}. The [[Marketing Accountability Standards Board (MASB)]] endorses the definitions, purposes, and constructs of classes of measures that appear in ''Marketing Metrics'' as part of its ongoing [http://www.commonlanguage.wikispaces.net/ Common Language in Marketing Project] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190405010451/https://www.commonlanguage.wikispaces.net/ |date=2019-04-05 }}.</ref><ref name=AMA>[[American Marketing Association]] Dictionary. {{cite web |url=http://www.marketingpower.com/_layouts/Dictionary.aspx |title=Dictionary |accessdate=2012-11-29 |url-status=dead |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20121121033809/http://www.marketingpower.com/_layouts/dictionary.aspx |archivedate=2012-11-21 }}. Retrieved 2013-2-11. The [[Marketing Accountability Standards Board (MASB)]] endorses this definition as part of its ongoing [http://www.commonlanguage.wikispaces.net/ Common Language in Marketing Project] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190405010451/https://www.commonlanguage.wikispaces.net/ |date=2019-04-05 }}.</ref>

GRPs are used predominantly as a measure of media with high ''potential'' exposures or [[Impression (online media)|impressions]]. [[Nielsen Media Research]] is an example of a company which uses GRPs.<ref>[https://www.nexttv.com/blog/ccpa-advertisers-media-measurement-own-hands Will CCPA Force Advertisers to Take Media Measurement Into Their Own Hands?] Published by Broadcasting + Cable on January 7, 2020, consulted on January 9, 2020</ref>

==Purpose==
With "today's fragmented media world" the value of GRP is, according to the [[Advertising Research Foundation]]'s ''Journal of Advertising Research'', even greater than in the pre-Internet era.<ref>{{cite journal 
   |journal=Journal of Advertising Research
   |title=Cross-Platform Advertising: Current Practices and Issues for the Future: Why the Gross Rating Point Metric Should Thrive in Today's Fragmented Media World
   |author1=P. Neijens  |author2=H. Voorveld |year=2015|doi=10.2501/JAR-2015-016
 |s2cid=167344548
 |url=https://pure.uva.nl/ws/files/2592337/168906_490856.pdf
 }}</ref> Since "the required frequency changes with the product and the competitive climate it is in",<ref name=GRP.NYT76/> the purpose of the GRP metric is to measure [[Impression (online media)|impressions]] compared to the number of people in the target for an advertising campaign.<ref name=Marketing_Metrics /> GRP values are commonly used by [[Media buying|media buyers]] to compare the advertising strength of components of a media plan.

For conventional media such as radio and TV, multi-tasking has reduced the value per GRP, and a measure named ''Persuasion Rating Point (PRP)'' was proposed in mid 2020.<ref>{{cite journal |journal=Journal of Advertising Research
|title=Effectiveness and Efficiency of TV's Brand-Building Power: A Historical Review: Why the Persuasion Rating Point (PRP) Is a More Accurate Metric than the GRP
|author1=F. Findley  |author2=K. Johnson  |author3=D. Crang
|url=http://www.journalofadvertisingresearch.com/content/early/2020/05/26/JAR-2020-011.abstract
|date=2020-05-26|doi=10.2501/JAR-2020-011
|s2cid=219770387
|url-access=subscription
}}</ref>

==Construction==
"One GRP is one percent of all potential adult television viewers (or in radio, listeners) in a market." If they are exposed to the ad three times, then that is 3 GRPs.<ref name=GRP.NYT76/>

GRPs are simply total impressions related to the size of the target population: They are most directly calculated by summing the ratings of individual ads in a campaign. 

Mathematically:
::GRPs (%)  = 100 * Total Impressions (#) ÷ Defined population (#)<ref name=Marketing_Metrics />
::GRPs (%)  = 100 * Reach (%) × Average frequency (#)

Three examples:
* If 100,000 ad impressions are displayed on multiple episodes or TV stations for a defined population of 100,000 people, the total is 100 GRPs. However, total [[Reach (advertising)|reach]] is not always 100%.
* If an average of 12% of the people view each episode of a television program, and an ad is placed on 5 episodes, then the campaign has 12 × 5 = 60 GRPs. 
* If 50% view three episodes, that's 150 GRPs.
